title: The United States and the Cold War
summary: World War II left only two true powers standing, and the wartime alliance between the United States and the Soviet Union quickly dissolved into rivalry. George Kennan's 1946 Long Telegram argued that Soviet expansion had to be checked, inspiring the policy of containment, and Churchill declared that an iron curtain had split Europe. In 1947 Truman cast aid to Greece and Turkey as a global defense of 'free peoples' against communism, while the Marshall Plan poured billions into rebuilding western Europe. The Soviets blockaded Berlin in 1948, prompting a year-long Allied airlift, and in 1949 the United States joined NATO, its first permanent European alliance. That same year the Soviets tested an atomic bomb and Mao's communists won China, spurring NSC-68's call for a massive military buildup. When North Korea invaded the South in 1950, U.S.-led UN forces fought a brutal three-year war ending in stalemate near the thirty-eighth parallel.

The Cold War became a contest over the meaning of freedom itself. Official culture equated Americanism with anticommunism and 'free enterprise,' while the concept of totalitarianism lumped the USSR with Nazi Germany. At home, Truman's Fair Deal—national health insurance, higher minimum wages, expanded Social Security—was mostly blocked by a conservative coalition, which also passed the anti-union Taft-Hartley Act over his veto after the huge 1946 strike wave. Yet Truman embraced civil rights as never before: his commission issued To Secure These Rights, he desegregated the armed forces in 1948, and the party's civil rights plank drove Strom Thurmond's Dixiecrats out of the convention. Truman still stunned pollsters by defeating Dewey in 1948.

Anticommunism also fueled a domestic purge. Truman's loyalty program, HUAC's Hollywood hearings and the blacklisting of the Hollywood Ten, the Hiss case, and the execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg fed a climate of fear that Senator Joseph McCarthy exploited with reckless, unproven charges of subversion. Loyalty oaths, the McCarran acts, and blacklists cost thousands of dissenters their jobs, purged militant unionists, and pushed civil rights groups to distance themselves from the left before McCarthy's televised downfall in 1954. The crusade narrowed the boundaries of acceptable dissent for a generation.
big_ideas: Containment—articulated in Kennan's Long Telegram and enacted through the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, and NSC-68—became the foundation of postwar American foreign policy.
The Korean War turned the Cold War hot and global, ending in stalemate but confirming America's commitment to fight communism anywhere.
Cold War ideology redefined American freedom around anticommunism and free enterprise, and the U.S. accepted undemocratic allies as members of the 'Free World.'
Truman's Fair Deal was largely blocked by a conservative Congress, and the Taft-Hartley Act began organized labor's long decline.
Truman's civil rights initiatives—To Secure These Rights and desegregation of the military—sparked the 1948 Dixiecrat revolt, an early sign of the South's coming realignment.
The second Red Scare, symbolized by McCarthyism, HUAC, and the Rosenberg case, punished dissent and violated civil liberties far beyond any real espionage threat.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) launched a global rights language, though both superpowers applied it selectively.

key_terms.def: The four-decade geopolitical and ideological struggle between the United States and the Soviet Union that began after World War II and shaped politics at home and abroad.
The core American strategy, derived from George Kennan's analysis, of blocking any further expansion of Soviet power rather than rolling it back or accommodating it.
Kennan's 1946 dispatch from Moscow arguing that Soviet ideology made normal diplomacy impossible and that the U.S. must firmly resist Soviet expansion.
Winston Churchill's 1946 phrase for the dividing line between the free West and Soviet-dominated eastern Europe.
Truman's 1947 pledge of aid to Greece and Turkey, framed as a worldwide American commitment to defend 'free peoples' against communism.
The massive 1947 U.S. aid program that rebuilt western European economies to blunt communism's appeal; the Soviets refused to participate, deepening Europe's division.
The 1948–1949 Soviet closure of land routes to West Berlin, answered by eleven months of Allied supply flights that forced Stalin to back down.
The 1949 mutual-defense alliance of the United States, Canada, and western Europe—America's first permanent European military commitment; the Soviets countered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955.
The secret 1950 policy paper that cast the Cold War as a struggle between freedom and slavery and called for a permanent, massive American military buildup.
The 1950–1953 conflict that began when communist North Korea invaded the South; U.S.-led UN forces and Chinese intervention produced a bloody stalemate ended by armistice, not a peace treaty.
Truman's domestic program of national health insurance, expanded Social Security, higher minimum wages, and civil rights, most of which a conservative Congress rejected.
The 1947 law passed over Truman's veto that banned the closed shop, allowed state 'right-to-work' laws, and curbed union power, contributing to labor's long-term decline.
Southern Democrats who bolted the 1948 convention over its civil rights plank and ran Strom Thurmond for president on a segregationist States' Rights ticket.
The post-1950 wave of reckless anticommunist accusation named for Senator Joseph McCarthy, whose unproven charges of subversion destroyed careers until his 1954 censure.
Screenwriters and directors jailed for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about their politics in 1947; the studios blacklisted them and hundreds of others.
The 1948 UN document, drafted under Eleanor Roosevelt, proclaiming political liberties and social-economic entitlements as rights belonging to all people everywhere.

timeline.event: Kennan's Long Telegram outlines containment and Churchill delivers his iron curtain speech; a giant postwar strike wave sweeps American industry.
Truman announces the Truman Doctrine, Marshall proposes his aid plan, Congress passes Taft-Hartley, HUAC investigates Hollywood, and Jackie Robinson integrates major league baseball.
Truman desegregates the armed forces, the Dixiecrats bolt over civil rights, the UN adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and Truman upsets Dewey.
The Soviets blockade Berlin, and Allied planes supply the city in an eleven-month airlift.
NATO is founded, the Soviet Union tests an atomic bomb, and Mao's communists win the Chinese civil war.
McCarthy claims communists riddle the State Department, NSC-68 urges a huge arms buildup, and North Korea's invasion of the South starts the Korean War.
Truman fires General MacArthur for insubordination, and Julius and Ethel Rosenberg are convicted of atomic espionage conspiracy.
The McCarran-Walter Act preserves national-origin immigration quotas and permits deportation of immigrant communists over Truman's veto.
An armistice halts the Korean War near the thirty-eighth parallel, and the Rosenbergs are executed.
The televised Army-McCarthy hearings expose McCarthy's bullying, and the Senate votes to condemn him.

themes: America in the world: The U.S. abandoned its aversion to permanent alliances, building a global network of aid, bases, and pacts to contain communism—even at the cost of backing undemocratic regimes and slowing decolonization.
Politics and power: A permanent national security state (CIA, NSC, loyalty programs) emerged, while McCarthyism showed how anticommunism could override civil liberties.

American and national identity: Freedom was redefined as the opposite of totalitarianism, and civil rights advocates argued that segregation damaged America's image in the battle for hearts and minds.
Work, exchange, and technology: Taft-Hartley and Operation Dixie's failure weakened labor, which traded militancy for private benefits, while military spending increasingly drove economic growth.
